units.translation: σῴζω: Didymus says σώζω without the iota, but the tradition has the iota. One must know that whenever it begins with the syllable σω followed by Ζ, it has the iota written adscript, σῴζω σῴζομαι ἔσωζον, but whenever it is not so, it is not written adscript, e.g. σαώζω σώσω σώσον
ἔσωζον, ἐσωζόμην, ἔσωσα, σώσω, σέσωσμαι, ἐσώθην [I was saving, I was being saved, I saved, I will save, I have been saved, I was saved]
σέσωται καὶ σεσωμένος: the ancients without the σ, and Thucydides says διεζωμένος [girded]

Triclinius, following Thomas Magister, interprets the manifestly corrupt reading as τὰ σώματα φθείρειν τῶν ὑπὸ χεῖρα [to destroy the bodies of those under one's power] and πόσιν [husband] (which Scaliger correctly wrote as ποσίν [with the feet]) with the addition of ἄνδρα ἁπλῶς [simply a man]. Schuetz's conjecture δωματοφθορεῖν ποσίν [to destroy the house with the feet], as Herodotus said οἰκοφθορεῖν [to ruin the household], is very easy but not very suitable to the sense. Without doubt one should write either στρωματοφθορεῖν [to destroy the bedding] with Auratus or, as Franz conjectured, εἱματοφθορεῖν [to destroy the clothing], although neither verb is known from elsewhere. The following φθείροντα [destroying] in the Florentine copy (for in the Medicean codex this part of the play is lost) is written φθάροντα, which Triclinius corrected following Thomas Magister, who explained it by καταναλίσκειν κακώς [to squander badly]. If Aeschylus wrote φθείροντα [destroying], it is strange that he preferred to use this verb after the preceding verb of the same root rather than another, such as πατοῦντα [trampling]: Hermann felt this, who conjectured στείβοντα [treading].
And as I tread upon these purple robes of the gods, may no envious eye strike me from afar; for there is great shame in destroying the body, destroying wealth and silver-bought fabrics.
